paragraphs.context: Finally Jack and Annie go to New York City
paragraphs.simple: The writer lived in New York City for over 25 years. It is a huge, busy city with skyscrapers, taxis, subways, parks and museums. She remembers a great blizzard in 1996: the city stopped, and after the storm everyone went out to play in the snow.

background.note: New York City is the biggest city in the USA, with more than 8 million people. It is famous for its skyscrapers, Central Park, museums and subway.
In January 1996 a huge blizzard dropped about 50 centimeters of snow on New York City, and the city stopped for days.

paragraphs.context: No matter what disasters it suffers, New York City always comes back.
paragraphs.simple: Even after very bad times, New York always gets better again. The writer hopes we enjoy the adventure.

paragraphs.context: One summer day, a mysterious tree house appeared in the woods.
paragraphs.mainIdea: How the tree house story began.
paragraphs.simple: A magic tree house appeared in the woods. It can take Jack and Annie to any time and place. It belongs to Morgan le Fay, a magic librarian from Camelot.

background.note: Morgan le Fay is a magic librarian from the King Arthur stories. The tree house belongs to her.
Camelot is the castle and city of King Arthur in the old stories. Merlin and Morgan live there.

paragraphs.context: After Jack and Annie traveled on many adventures for Morgan
paragraphs.simple: Later, Merlin the magician sent them on "Merlin Missions". Teddy and Kathleen, two young sorcerers, helped them find things to save Camelot.

background.note: Teddy is a young sorcerer and Kathleen is a "selkie" (a seal girl). Both learn magic in Camelot and wrote the book of magic rhymes for Jack and Annie.

paragraphs.context: For their next four Merlin Missions, Jack and Annie were told
paragraphs.simple: On these four missions they must show Merlin they can use magic wisely in real places in history. They have been to Venice, Baghdad and Paris. Now they wait for Merlin again.

background.note: Venice, Baghdad and Paris were Jack and Annie's last three missions: Venice in the 1740s, Baghdad about 1,200 years ago, and the Paris World's Fair of 1889.

paragraphs.context: The November sky was gray with clouds.
paragraphs.simple: It is a gray November day. Jack is reading by the fire at home.

paragraphs.context: “Who wants hot chocolate?” his dad called from the kitchen.
paragraphs.simple: Dad is making hot chocolate.

paragraphs.context: The front door burst open, and with a gust of cold wind
paragraphs.simple: Annie rushes in with a cold wind. She whispers that the tree house is back.

paragraphs.context: “I was walking home from the library”
paragraphs.simple: Annie saw a flash in the sky over the woods. That happened last time too.

paragraphs.context: Before she could finish the sentence, Jack jumped up.
paragraphs.simple: Jack jumps up and asks Dad to wait with the hot chocolate.

paragraphs.simple: Jack goes to get his backpack.

paragraphs.simple: Annie reminds him to bring the rhyme book.

paragraphs.simple: Jack takes his backpack and checks that the rhyme book is inside.

paragraphs.context: Jack charged back downstairs.
paragraphs.simple: Jack puts on his boots, jacket, scarf and mittens and runs out.

paragraphs.simple: It is so cold that Jack can see his breath.

paragraphs.simple: They run into the woods. Their boots crunch on the dry leaves.

paragraphs.simple: The tree house is in the tall oak again. Jack tells Annie she was right.

paragraphs.simple: They climb the rope ladder.

paragraphs.simple: They find a book and a scroll. Annie reads it aloud.

paragraphs.simple: Annie already loves the unicorn and wants to show him the way.

paragraphs.context: “But this poem is really hard to understand,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack thinks the poem is hard to understand. He looks at the research book.

paragraphs.simple: Annie remembers a visit to New York with Aunt Mallory.

paragraphs.simple: A unicorn is from old stories. New York is a real city, and 1938 is not very long ago. Jack is puzzled.

paragraphs.simple: Annie reminds Jack that they have the magic rhymes.

paragraphs.simple: The first one is "Pull a Cloud from the Sky".

paragraphs.simple: Jack is not sure the cloud rhyme will help. The next is "Find a Treasure You Must Never Lose".

Central Park is a huge park in the middle of New York City, about 4 kilometers long. It opened in the 1850s and 1860s.

paragraphs.simple: New York is the biggest city in the Americas.

paragraphs.simple: A blue moon is the second full moon in one month. It does not happen often.

paragraphs.context: “Right,” said Jack. “Okay. Let’s review:
paragraphs.simple: The unicorn is on public display and under a spell. Before the blue moon they must call his name. Then Annie must love him and show him the way home.

background.note: A MetroCard was a plastic card used to pay for New York subways and buses. Since about 2019 the city has been changing to tap-to-pay cards and phones.

paragraphs.context: Central Park: Today, more than 250,000 people might visit Central Park
paragraphs.simple: Many people enjoy Central Park. It was the first big park made for everyone. Its designers believed nature makes city people happier.

background.term: Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux
background.note: They designed Central Park in 1858. Olmsted later designed many other famous American parks.

paragraphs.context: Belvedere Castle: Today, Belvedere Castle in Central Park
paragraphs.simple: Belvedere Castle is now a nature center. Weather tools there still measure the temperature in Central Park.

paragraphs.context: John D. Rockefeller: Today, America remembers John D. Rockefeller
paragraphs.simple: Rockefeller was once the richest man in America and gave away half his money. His son helped make the Cloisters museum.

background.note: Standard Oil was John D. Rockefeller's oil company, started in 1870. It became one of the biggest companies in the world.
Fort Tryon Park is a park in the north of Manhattan. The Cloisters museum stands in it.

paragraphs.context: The Cloisters: Today, the Cloisters is filled with approximately 5,000 works
paragraphs.simple: The Cloisters has about 5,000 works of art from the Middle Ages, including the Unicorn Tapestries.

background.note: The Unicorn Tapestries are seven large wall hangings made in Europe around 1500. They show people hunting a unicorn. You can see them at the Cloisters.

paragraphs.context: Unicorns: Today, unicorns appear in old stories
paragraphs.simple: Unicorns are in old stories from many countries, but there is no proof they were real.

background.note: A rhinoceros (rhino) is a large, heavy animal from Africa and Asia. Some rhinos have one horn on the nose.

sentences.context: A brother and sister named Jack and Annie soon learned that the tree house was magic—it could take them to any time and any place in history.
sentences.simple: Jack and Annie, a brother and sister, found out that the tree house was magic. It could take them to any time and place in the past.
sentences.main: Jack and Annie learned that the tree house was magic.

parts.text: A brother and sister named Jack and Annie
parts.meaning: Jack and Annie, brother and sister,

parts.text: soon learned that the tree house was magic—
parts.meaning: quickly found out the tree house was magic.

parts.text: it could take them to any time and any place in history.
parts.job: What the magic does (after the dash).
parts.meaning: It could take them anywhere in the past.

sentences.grammar: The dash (—) adds an explanation: it tells us what kind of magic the tree house has.

sentences.context: With help from two young sorcerers named Teddy and Kathleen, Jack and Annie visited four mythical places and found valuable objects to help save Camelot.
sentences.simple: Teddy and Kathleen, two young magicians, helped them. Jack and Annie went to four places from old stories and found important things to save Camelot.
sentences.main: Jack and Annie visited four mythical places.

parts.text: With help from two young sorcerers named Teddy and Kathleen,
Jack and Annie visited four mythical places
parts.meaning: Jack and Annie went to four places from old stories

parts.text: and found valuable objects to help save Camelot.
parts.job: What else they did, and why.
parts.meaning: and found important things to save Camelot.

sentences.grammar: "To help save" tells the reason (why they found the objects).

sentences.context: For their next four Merlin Missions, Jack and Annie were told they must travel to real times and real places in history and prove to Merlin that they could use magic wisely.
sentences.simple: For the next four missions, Jack and Annie had to go to real places in the past and show Merlin that they could use magic well.
sentences.main: Jack and Annie were told they must travel to real places in history.

parts.text: For their next four Merlin Missions,
Jack and Annie were told
they must travel to real times and real places in history
parts.meaning: they had to go to real places in the past

parts.text: and prove to Merlin that they could use magic wisely.
parts.meaning: and show Merlin they could use magic in a smart way.

sentences.grammar: "Were told" is passive: we don't say who told them. "Must travel ... and prove" are two things they have to do.

sentences.context: He pulled on his boots, put on his jacket, tied a scarf around his neck, grabbed his mittens, and headed out the door.

sentences.main: He headed out the door.

put on his jacket,
tied a scarf around his neck,
grabbed his mittens,
and headed out the door.

sentences.context: When they climbed inside the tree house, Jack and Annie saw a book and a scroll of parchment paper lying on the floor.
sentences.simple: Inside the tree house, Jack and Annie saw a book and a rolled-up old paper on the floor.
sentences.main: Jack and Annie saw a book and a scroll.

parts.text: When they climbed inside the tree house,
parts.meaning: When they got into the tree house,

parts.text: Jack and Annie saw a book and a scroll of parchment paper
parts.meaning: they saw a book and a rolled paper

parts.text: lying on the floor.

sentences.grammar: "Lying on the floor" describes the book and the scroll: where they were.

sentences.context: Jack tried to keep walking in a straight line, but the path they were following began twisting and turning like a maze.
sentences.simple: Jack wanted to walk straight, but the path turned this way and that way, like a maze.
sentences.main: The path began twisting and turning.

parts.text: Jack tried to keep walking in a straight line,
but the path they were following
began twisting and turning like a maze.
parts.meaning: turned again and again like a maze.

sentences.grammar: "But" shows the opposite of what Jack wanted. "They were following" describes the path.

sentences.context: He could barely make out two figures in the snow: one in a dark cape and one in a raincoat.
sentences.simple: He could just see two people in the snow. One wore a dark cape and one wore a raincoat.
sentences.main: He could barely make out two figures.

parts.text: He could barely make out two figures in the snow:
parts.meaning: He could only just see two people in the snow.

parts.text: one in a dark cape and one in a raincoat.
parts.meaning: One wore a dark cape, one a raincoat.

sentences.grammar: "Make out" means see with difficulty. The colon (:) introduces the details.

sentences.context: They passed an old man and woman huddled in a doorway, wrapped in torn blankets, burning a fire in a small stove.
sentences.simple: They walked past an old man and woman sitting close together in a doorway, in old blankets, with a small fire.
sentences.main: They passed an old man and woman.

parts.text: They passed an old man and woman
parts.meaning: They walked past an old man and woman

parts.meaning: sitting close together in a doorway,

parts.text: wrapped in torn blankets,
burning a fire in a small stove.
parts.meaning: with a fire in a small stove.

sentences.grammar: Three describing phrases ("huddled", "wrapped", "burning") tell us about the old man and woman.

sentences.context: In the 1930s, New York City, as well as the rest of the United States, suffered through hard times known as the Great Depression.
sentences.simple: In the 1930s, New York and all of the USA had a very hard time called the Great Depression.
sentences.main: New York City suffered through hard times.

parts.text: In the 1930s,
New York City, as well as the rest of the United States,
parts.meaning: New York and all of the USA

parts.text: suffered through hard times
known as the Great Depression.

sentences.grammar: "As well as" means "and also". "Known as" gives the name.

sentences.context: Jack and Annie watched an old woman put her nickel in the slot of the turnstile, which led to the train platform.
sentences.simple: Jack and Annie watched an old woman put a coin into the gate machine that let people go to the trains.
sentences.main: Jack and Annie watched an old woman.

parts.text: Jack and Annie watched an old woman
parts.meaning: Jack and Annie watched an old woman

parts.text: put her nickel in the slot of the turnstile,
parts.meaning: put a coin into the gate

parts.text: which led to the train platform.

sentences.grammar: "Watched someone put" uses the base verb after "watched". "Which led" tells us more about the turnstile.

sentences.context: They held on to a silver pole as more riders squeezed into the subway car and grabbed straps hanging overhead.
sentences.simple: They held a silver pole while more people pushed into the train and held straps above them.
sentences.main: They held on to a silver pole.

parts.text: They held on to a silver pole
as more riders squeezed into the subway car
parts.meaning: while more people pushed into the train

parts.text: and grabbed straps hanging overhead.
parts.meaning: and held straps above their heads.

sentences.grammar: "As" here means "at the same time as".

sentences.context: When the train stopped and the doors opened, Jack and Annie were practically pushed out onto the platform with the other people leaving.
sentences.simple: When the train stopped, the crowd almost pushed Jack and Annie out of the train with them.
sentences.main: Jack and Annie were practically pushed out.

parts.text: When the train stopped and the doors opened,
parts.meaning: When the train stopped and the doors opened,

parts.text: Jack and Annie were practically pushed out onto the platform
parts.meaning: Jack and Annie were almost pushed out

parts.text: with the other people leaving.

sentences.grammar: "Were pushed" is passive: the crowd pushed them. "Practically" means "almost".

sentences.context: The taxi motor kept running, but the wheels only spun in place, sending up sprays of dirty snow.
sentences.simple: The engine was on, but the wheels just turned without moving the car and threw dirty snow into the air.
sentences.main: The wheels only spun in place.

parts.text: The taxi motor kept running,
but the wheels only spun in place,
parts.meaning: but the wheels turned without going anywhere,

parts.text: sending up sprays of dirty snow.

sentences.grammar: "Kept running" means did not stop. "Sending up" shows the result of the spinning wheels.

sentences.context: When they came to a door, Jack pushed it open, and he and Annie slipped out of the cold into a large, warm room.
sentences.simple: At a door, Jack pushed it open, and they quickly went from the cold into a big, warm room.
sentences.main: He and Annie slipped into a large, warm room.

parts.text: When they came to a door,
Jack pushed it open,
and he and Annie slipped out of the cold into a large, warm room.
parts.meaning: and they quietly went in from the cold to a big warm room.

sentences.grammar: "Out of ... into ..." shows movement from one place to another.

sentences.context: The other tapestries showed the unicorn trying to escape, leaping from a stream, chased by hounds, then captured and slain by the hunters’ spears.
sentences.simple: The other wall pictures showed the unicorn trying to run away, jumping from a stream, chased by dogs, and then caught and killed by the hunters.
sentences.main: The other tapestries showed the unicorn.

parts.text: The other tapestries showed the unicorn
parts.meaning: The other tapestries showed the unicorn

parts.text: trying to escape,
leaping from a stream,
chased by hounds,
then captured and slain by the hunters’ spears.
parts.meaning: then caught and killed by the hunters.

sentences.grammar: The phrases tell the story in order. "Chased", "captured" and "slain" are passive: someone did these things to the unicorn.

sentences.context: At that moment, there was a flash of light, and the unicorn in the tapestry leapt like a deer over the woven fence.
sentences.simple: Just then, there was a flash of light, and the unicorn jumped like a deer over the fence in the tapestry.
sentences.main: The unicorn leapt over the woven fence.

parts.text: At that moment,
there was a flash of light,
and the unicorn in the tapestry leapt like a deer over the woven fence.
parts.meaning: and the unicorn jumped like a deer over the fence.

sentences.grammar: "Leapt" is the past of "leap". "Like a deer" compares how he jumped.

sentences.context: But standing on the floor of the museum was the most beautiful creature Jack had ever seen.
sentences.simple: On the museum floor stood the most beautiful animal Jack had ever seen.
sentences.main: The most beautiful creature was standing on the floor.

parts.text: But standing on the floor of the museum
was the most beautiful creature
Jack had ever seen.

sentences.grammar: The order is turned around for surprise: normally "The most beautiful creature was standing on the floor."

sentences.context: Feeling their way along the walkway, they came to the door that led to the main hall.
sentences.simple: They touched things to find their way along the path and came to the door to the main hall.
sentences.main: They came to the door.

parts.text: Feeling their way along the walkway,
parts.meaning: Touching things to find the way,

parts.text: they came to the door
that led to the main hall.

sentences.grammar: "Feeling their way" means moving slowly and touching things because you cannot see.

sentences.context: As he moved past old mansions, broken-down tenements, and shabby hotels, people peeked out of doorways and windows to see why the sounds of the storm had died away.
sentences.simple: He went past big old houses, poor old apartment buildings and dirty hotels. People looked out to see why the storm had become quiet.
sentences.main: People peeked out of doorways and windows.

parts.text: As he moved past old mansions, broken-down tenements, and shabby hotels,
parts.meaning: As he passed rich and poor buildings,

parts.text: people peeked out of doorways and windows
parts.meaning: people looked out of doors and windows

parts.text: to see why the sounds of the storm had died away.
parts.meaning: to find out why the storm was quiet.

sentences.grammar: "Had died away" (past perfect) happened before they looked. "To see" tells the reason.

sentences.context: When they caught sight of Dianthus, with his horn shining in the windless air, they broke into joyful smiles.
sentences.simple: When they saw Dianthus with his shining horn, they suddenly smiled happily.
sentences.main: They broke into joyful smiles.

parts.text: When they caught sight of Dianthus,
with his horn shining in the windless air,
they broke into joyful smiles.

sentences.grammar: "Caught sight of" means suddenly saw. "Broke into" means suddenly started.

sentences.context: When they rode past the merry-go-round, Jack heard a chorus of neighs and whinnies accompanied by lively carousel music.
sentences.simple: Riding past the carousel, Jack heard many horse sounds together with happy carousel music.
sentences.main: Jack heard a chorus of neighs and whinnies.

parts.text: When they rode past the merry-go-round,
Jack heard a chorus of neighs and whinnies
accompanied by lively carousel music.

sentences.grammar: "Neighs" and "whinnies" are horse sounds. "Accompanied by" means "together with".

sentences.context: Jack saw a blur of colors: gray and brown, green and white, a dash of orange, a dash of yellow.
sentences.simple: Jack saw colors moving too fast to see clearly: gray, brown, green, white, a little orange and a little yellow.
sentences.main: Jack saw a blur of colors.

parts.text: Jack saw a blur of colors:
gray and brown, green and white,
a dash of orange, a dash of yellow.
parts.meaning: a little orange and a little yellow.

sentences.grammar: The colon (:) introduces a list. "A dash of" means a small amount of.

sentences.context: The back door of the car opened, and two grown-ups stepped out: a tall, elegant woman wearing a wine-colored cloak and a man in a dark blue robe.
sentences.simple: Two adults got out of the back of the car: a tall, beautiful woman in a dark red cloak and a man in a dark blue robe.
sentences.main: Two grown-ups stepped out.

parts.text: The back door of the car opened,
and two grown-ups stepped out:
a tall, elegant woman wearing a wine-colored cloak
parts.meaning: a tall, beautiful woman in a dark red cloak

parts.text: and a man in a dark blue robe.
parts.meaning: and a man in a dark blue robe.

sentences.grammar: The colon (:) introduces the two people. "Wine-colored" means dark red.

sentences.context: As the wizard and magical librarian of Camelot walked across the snow, Dianthus stepped forward to greet them.
sentences.simple: While Merlin and Morgan walked across the snow, Dianthus walked toward them to say hello.
sentences.main: Dianthus stepped forward to greet them.

parts.text: As the wizard and magical librarian of Camelot walked across the snow,
parts.meaning: While Merlin and Morgan walked over the snow,

parts.text: Dianthus stepped forward to greet them.
parts.meaning: Dianthus went to say hello to them.

sentences.grammar: "The wizard and magical librarian of Camelot" means Merlin and Morgan. "To greet" tells why he stepped forward.

sentences.context: As the cold wind rattled the bare trees of the Frog Creek woods, Jack and Annie hurried home.
sentences.simple: While the cold wind shook the trees with no leaves, Jack and Annie went home quickly.
sentences.main: Jack and Annie hurried home.

parts.text: As the cold wind rattled the bare trees of the Frog Creek woods,
parts.meaning: While the cold wind shook the bare trees,

parts.text: Jack and Annie hurried home.
parts.meaning: Jack and Annie went home fast.

sentences.grammar: "Rattled" means shook and made a noise. "Bare trees" have no leaves.
